**On 20 July 2007 an aeroplane weighing about as much as three passengers took off from Rogers Dry Lake, and the number that matters about it is 240.** The X-48B spans 20.4 feet. The aeroplane it was built to describe spans 240 feet, and every claim the programme made about that larger machine had to travel across a factor of 8.5 percent to get there [[Regan, In-flight stability analysis of the X-48B aircraft][research_regan_x48b_stability]].

[X-46][related_post_a343_boeing_x46], and the [X-47][related_post_a344_northrop_grumman_x47].

**This is a full-length article and the record supports the length.** Two airframes flew 122 times over six years, in two configurations, through envelope expansion, parameter identification, engine-out testing and deliberate approaches to the limit of controlled flight [[X-48 Research, All Good Things Must Come to an End, NASA][ref_nasa_x48_end]].

**It is also the first aeroplane in this series whose central question is about the instrument rather than the vehicle.** The previous three articles were unmanned combat aircraft. This one is a transport configuration, and the interesting thing about it is not what it did but what its size permits anyone to conclude.

## The Research Question

**The blended wing body was never in doubt at cruise, and was entirely in doubt on approach.** The configuration's case is aerodynamic efficiency, and by the time the X-48 flew, the cruise argument had been made in analysis and in the tunnel [[Liebeck, Design of the blended wing body subsonic transport][research_liebeck_bwb]]. What no tunnel settles is whether a large tailless aeroplane with twenty trailing-edge surfaces and no horizontal tail can be flown safely at low speed by a line pilot, and where it stops being controllable.

**A free-flight model answers that question, and it answers it by giving something up.** A model cannot match every dimensionless group at once. Matching the ratio of inertial to gravitational force, which is the Froude number, makes the model move like the aeroplane. Matching the ratio of inertial to viscous force, which is the Reynolds number, makes the air behave around the model as it does around the aeroplane. **At any scale below one, those two demands conflict, and the free-flight tradition resolves the conflict in favour of Froude** [[Chambers, Modeling flight, the role of dynamically scaled free-flight models in support of NASA's aerospace programs][research_chambers_modeling_flight]].

**So the question this article asks is what the X-48B's scale factor bought and what it cost.** The answer is arithmetic rather than opinion, and it turns out to bear directly on the single most quoted result of the flight programme.

## Programme Origin

**Four scaled blended wing bodies preceded the answer, and two of them never flew.** The designation record for the whole family is set out in the specialist directory [[Parsch, Boeing X-48, Directory of U.S. Military Rockets and Missiles][ref_parsch_x48]], and the general configuration has a literature of its own reaching back to the tailless transports of the 1940s [[Wooldridge, Winged wonders, the story of the flying wings][book_wooldridge]] [[Blended wing body][ref_bwb_wikipedia]].

The first was the BWB-17, a 17-foot-span model weighing 120 pounds, built at Stanford University under NASA sponsorship and flown on 29 July 1997 at El Mirage Dry Lake. It was dynamically scaled, carried an onboard computer for stability augmentation, and demonstrated good handling qualities within the normal envelope [[Liebeck, Design of the blended wing body subsonic transport][research_liebeck_bwb]].

The second was the X-48A. In 2000 NASA and Boeing began a 35-foot-span remotely piloted model, and the designation was allocated in late 2001. **After about a year the programme was cancelled and NASA redirected its effort to a 12-foot-span free-flight model for the Langley Full-Scale Tunnel** [[Chambers, Modeling flight, the role of dynamically scaled free-flight models in support of NASA's aerospace programs][research_chambers_modeling_flight]]. **That redirection is the most consequential decision in this article, and the section on scaling prices it.**

The third and fourth are the aeroplanes that flew. Boeing Phantom Works took the lead on the X-48B in 2006 with NASA and the Air Force Research Laboratory [[Boeing Phantom Works to lead research on X-48B blended wing body concept][ref_boeing_x48b_release]] [[X-48 Blended Wing Body, GlobalSecurity][ref_x48_globalsecurity]]. Two X-48B airframes were built by Cranfield Aerospace in the United Kingdom to Boeing's specifications [[Cranfield Aerospace Solutions][ref_cranfield_aerospace]] [[Boeing X-48][ref_x48_wikipedia]]. Ship 1 went to the Langley Full-Scale Tunnel for 250 hours of testing in May 2006, and Ship 2 became the flight vehicle [[X-48 Hybrid/Blended Wing Body, NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-090][ref_nasa_fs090]]. Ship 2 was later rebuilt as the X-48C.

## The Scaling Decision, Which Is the Whole Article

### The Geometry Closes Exactly

**Two numbers are published independently and their ratio is not approximate.** NASA states the X-48B as an 8.5 percent scale vehicle, and separately states a span of 20.4 feet against a notional full-scale span of 240 feet. Taking the ratio,

$$n = \frac{20.4\ \text{ft}}{240\ \text{ft}} = 0.085000$$

**which agrees with the published 8.5 percent to fourteen decimal places.** That is worth stating because it establishes that the reference vehicle is a real design with a fixed span rather than a round number attached afterwards, and every relation below inherits that exactness.

### What Froude Matching Does to Everything Else

**Two dimensionless groups compete and only one can be held.** The Froude number is the ratio of inertial to gravitational force and the Reynolds number is the ratio of inertial to viscous force,

$$Fr = \frac{V^{2}}{Lg}, \qquad Re = \frac{VL}{\nu}$$

**Setting the model's Froude number equal to the aeroplane's is what fixes the speed ratio**, and it does so without reference to the air at all,

$$\frac{V_m^{2}}{L_m g} = \frac{V_f^{2}}{L_f g} \implies r_V = \frac{V_m}{V_f} = \sqrt{\frac{L_m}{L_f}} = \sqrt{n}$$

**The mass condition is a separate requirement and it is the one usually forgotten.** A dynamic model must also match the relative density factor, which compares the model's mass to the air it displaces,

$$\sigma = \frac{m}{\rho l^{3}}$$

so that the weight ratio carries an atmospheric term,

$$r_W = \frac{n^{3}}{\sigma}$$

**When the model and the aeroplane fly in the same air, $\sigma$ is one and the term disappears.** The article returns to what happens when they do not.

Holding the Froude number and the relative density fixed determines every other ratio by dimensions alone. With $n$ the length ratio and the model flying in the same air as the aeroplane,

$$r_V = \sqrt{n}, \qquad r_t = \sqrt{n}, \qquad r_\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}$$

$$r_W = n^3, \qquad r_I = n^5, \qquad r_{Re} = n^{3/2}$$

**The Reynolds ratio is not an independent choice but a consequence**, being the product of the speed ratio already fixed by Froude and the length ratio,

$$r_{Re} = r_V \, r_L = n^{1/2} \cdot n = n^{3/2}$$

**and that single line is the whole cost of the decision.** Two further ratios follow the same way and both matter later. The dynamic pressure and the wing loading go as

$$r_q = \frac{\rho V_m^{2}}{\rho V_f^{2}} = r_V^{2} = n, \qquad r_{W/S} = \frac{n^{3}}{n^{2}} = n$$

**The weight goes as the cube because it is a force and a force at matched Froude number scales as $\rho V^2 L^2$, which is $n \cdot n^2$.** The underlying rigid-body equations are standard [[Etkin and Reid, Dynamics of flight][book_etkin_reid]] [[McCormick, Aerodynamics, aeronautics and flight mechanics][book_mccormick]]. The Reynolds ratio is the product of the velocity ratio and the length ratio, which is where the three halves comes from.

At $n = 0.085$ these evaluate to the following.

| Quantity | Ratio | Value at 8.5 percent |
|---|---|---|
| Length | $n$ | 0.0850 |
| Velocity | $n^{1/2}$ | 0.2915 |
| Time | $n^{1/2}$ | 0.2915 |
| Angular rate | $n^{-1/2}$ | 3.430 |
| Weight and force | $n^{3}$ | $6.141 \times 10^{-4}$ |
| Moment of inertia | $n^{5}$ | $4.437 \times 10^{-6}$ |
| Reynolds number | $n^{3/2}$ | 0.02478 |
| Thrust to weight | $1$ | 1.000 |

**Two rows carry the argument.** The model's angular motions run **3.430 times faster** than the aeroplane's, and the model's Reynolds number is **1/40.35 of the aeroplane's**.

### The Pilot Does Not Scale

**Time compression is a statement about the pilot as much as about the aeroplane.** Any interval scales as

$$t_m = t_f \sqrt{n} = 0.2915 \, t_f$$

so a motion that the full-scale aeroplane would develop over three seconds develops in the model in

$$t_m = 3 \times 0.2915 = 0.875\ \text{s}$$

**and the angular rates that go with it are faster by the reciprocal,**

$$r_\omega = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} = 3.430$$

The aeroplane is on a dry lake bed and the pilot is in a ground station, and **the pilot's reaction time is not multiplied by 0.2915 to match.**

NASA's own account of dynamic model testing states the problem plainly, noting that because a model's angular motions are so much faster than the aeroplane's, the models may be difficult to control, and that the response has often been to share the piloting task among more than one person [[Chambers, Modeling flight, the role of dynamically scaled free-flight models in support of NASA's aerospace programs][research_chambers_modeling_flight]].

**This series has measured this before at a gentler scale.** The [X-36][related_post_a333_mcdonnell_douglas_x36] was a 28 percent remotely piloted tailless demonstrator, and the same relations give a time compression of 1.890 and a Reynolds penalty of 6.75. Against it,

$$\frac{r_t^{-1}(0.085)}{r_t^{-1}(0.28)} = 1.815, \qquad \frac{r_{Re}^{-1}(0.085)}{r_{Re}^{-1}(0.28)} = 5.979$$

**The X-48B's pilot faced dynamics 1.815 times faster than the X-36's, and its aerodynamics were 5.979 times further from full scale.** The X-36 article argued that a scale factor is a statement about what an experiment is able to measure. This is the same statement at nearly twice the severity.

### Reynolds Number in Absolute Terms, and the Altitude That Makes It Worse

**A ratio of 40.35 says nothing about where either aeroplane sits**, and the absolute values decide whether the mismatch matters. Using a reference chord and the published maximum speed of 118 knots,

$$Re = \frac{V c}{\nu}, \qquad c = \frac{S}{b} = \frac{100.5}{20.4} = 4.926\ \text{ft}$$

**The wing area here comes from a secondary compilation and not from a primary source**, which the article flags rather than hides. **The ratio below does not depend on it**, because the chord cancels.

At sea level, with $\nu_0 = 1.5723 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{ft}^2/\text{s}$,

$$Re_{\text{model}} = \frac{199.2 \times 4.926}{1.5723 \times 10^{-4}} = 6.24 \times 10^{6}$$

and the corresponding full-scale condition, at $V_f = V_m/\sqrt{n}$ and $c_f = c/n$,

$$Re_{\text{full}} = \frac{683.1 \times 58.0}{1.5723 \times 10^{-4}} = 2.52 \times 10^{8}$$

**Both are above the range where a boundary layer is deciding whether to be turbulent at all, and they are two orders of magnitude apart.**

**The published speed also checks the scaling.** Inverting the speed ratio on the model's maximum,

$$V_f = \frac{118}{\sqrt{0.085}} = 404.7\ \text{kt}$$

**which is a sensible cruise speed for a large subsonic transport**, and is therefore a second piece of evidence that the reference vehicle is real rather than nominal.

**The atmosphere then makes the mismatch worse, and this is the one place the standard atmosphere earns its keep in this article.** The model flew to a ceiling of 10,000 feet while the full-scale aeroplane's low-speed regime is near the ground. Kinematic viscosity rises with altitude,

$$\nu(h) = \frac{\mu(h)}{\rho(h)}, \qquad \frac{\nu(10{,}000)}{\nu(0)} = \frac{2.0135 \times 10^{-4}}{1.5723 \times 10^{-4}} = 1.281$$

so a model tested at its ceiling against an aeroplane approaching at sea level suffers

$$P_{\text{effective}} = n^{-3/2} \times \frac{\nu(10{,}000)}{\nu(0)} = 40.35 \times 1.281 = 51.7$$

**The honest penalty is therefore between 40.35 and 51.7 depending on the test altitude**, and the larger figure is the one that applies to any manoeuvre flown high.

### What Cancelling the X-48A Cost

**The penalty is a function of span alone once the reference is fixed**, since $n = b/b_{\text{ref}}$ gives

$$P(b) = \left(\frac{b_{\text{ref}}}{b}\right)^{3/2}, \qquad \tau(b) = \left(\frac{b_{\text{ref}}}{b}\right)^{1/2}$$

The three scaled vehicles NASA considered against the same 240-foot reference price out as follows.

| Vehicle | Span | Scale | Time compression | Reynolds penalty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X-48A, planned and cancelled | 35 ft | 0.1458 | 2.619 | 17.96 |
| X-48B, flown | 20.4 ft | 0.0850 | 3.430 | 40.35 |
| Langley free-flight model | 12 ft | 0.0500 | 4.472 | 89.44 |

**The cost of the substitution is a ratio of two such penalties and needs no other quantity,**

$$\frac{P(20.4)}{P(35)} = \left(\frac{35}{20.4}\right)^{3/2} = 2.247, \qquad \frac{\tau(20.4)}{\tau(35)} = \left(\frac{35}{20.4}\right)^{1/2} = 1.310$$

**Cancelling the 35-foot aeroplane and flying the 20.4-foot one multiplied the Reynolds shortfall by 2.247 and made the aeroplane 31 percent quicker in its own time.** That is the price of the 2002 decision, stated in the only units in which it can be stated. **It is not an argument that the decision was wrong**, since a 35-foot vehicle is a different programme in cost, airspace and risk, but it is the quantity the decision traded.

### What the Model's Own Weight Says About the Vehicle It Represents

**A dynamically scaled model is weight-scaled, so the relation can be run backwards.** Taking the maximum weight of 525 pounds and inverting the cube,

$$W_{\text{full}} = \frac{525\ \text{lb}}{n^3} = 8.549 \times 10^{5}\ \text{lb}$$

**That figure assumes $\sigma = 1$, and the relative density factor is exactly the term the earlier section set aside.** Restoring it,

$$W_{\text{full}} = \frac{W_m}{n^{3}} \cdot \frac{\rho_f}{\rho_m}$$

and evaluating for three readings of where the model's condition sits,

| Model condition | $\rho_m/\rho_0$ | Implied full-scale weight |
|---|---|---|
| same air as the aeroplane | 1.0000 | 854,875 lb |
| Rogers Dry Lake, 2,300 ft | 0.9344 | 914,885 lb |
| ceiling, 10,000 ft | 0.7385 | 1,157,634 lb |

**So 854,875 pounds is a lower bound rather than an estimate**, and the article uses it as one.

**No source in the record states the reference vehicle's weight, so this is a derived figure and the article treats it as one.** It can nevertheless be tested. Liebeck's published second-generation blended wing body carries a maximum takeoff gross weight of 823,000 pounds, and the BWB-450 baseline spans 249 feet [[Liebeck, Design of the blended wing body subsonic transport][research_liebeck_bwb]]. Scaling that design geometrically to a 240-foot span,

$$W(240) = 823{,}000 \times \left(\frac{240}{249}\right)^{3} = 736{,}946\ \text{lb}$$

gives a comparison of

$$\frac{W_{\text{full}}}{W(240)} = \frac{854{,}875}{736{,}946} = 1.160$$

so the vehicle implied by the model's own weight is **at least 1.160 times heavier than a passenger blended wing body of the same span**, and **1.241 times heavier on the field-elevation reading.**

**That is the right direction and about the right size.** The Air Force's stated interest was a multi-role, long-range, high-capacity military transport [[X-48 Hybrid/Blended Wing Body, NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-090][ref_nasa_fs090]], and a freighter is denser than an airliner of the same dimensions, as the conventional airlifter it would replace already shows [[Boeing C-17 Globemaster III][ref_c17_wikipedia]]. The weight relations that make that comparison meaningful are the standard conceptual-design ones [[Raymer, Aircraft design, a conceptual approach][book_raymer]] [[Torenbeek, Synthesis of subsonic airplane design][book_torenbeek]] [[Nicolai and Carichner, Fundamentals of aircraft and airship design][book_nicolai]]. **The model's weight is therefore consistent with a military reference vehicle and not with the commercial one**, which is a fact about the programme recoverable from nothing but the scale relations.

### Thrust Is Invariant Under Froude Scaling and This Model Does Not Match It

**Thrust is a force, so it scales as $n^3$, and thrust to weight is therefore the same number for the model and the aeroplane.** That makes it directly checkable.

$$\left(\frac{T}{W}\right)_{\text{model}} = \frac{3 \times 54\ \text{lbf}}{525\ \text{lb}} = 0.3086$$

$$\left(\frac{T}{W}\right)_{\text{full}} = \frac{3 \times 61{,}600\ \text{lbf}}{823{,}000\ \text{lb}} = 0.2245$$

$$\frac{(T/W)_{\text{model}}}{(T/W)_{\text{full}}} = \frac{0.3086}{0.2245} = 1.374$$

**The model carries 1.374 times the thrust to weight of the aeroplane it represents.** This is not a defect. A model that must take off from a lake bed, climb to a test altitude inside a small working area and go around from an approach needs margin the transport does not.

**But it means the demonstration is tilted, and the direction is computable.** Thrust to weight is one of the handful of ratios that fixes an aeroplane's performance at all [[Anderson, Aircraft performance and design][book_anderson_performance]].

**The quantity that matters for engine-out is the asymmetric thrust carried as a fraction of weight**, which for $N_e$ equal engines with one failed is

$$\frac{\Delta T}{W} = \frac{T}{W} \cdot \frac{1}{N_e}$$

**Evaluating for the two models and for the full-scale trijet,**

$$\left(\frac{\Delta T}{W}\right)_{B} = \frac{0.3086}{3} = 0.10286, \qquad \left(\frac{\Delta T}{W}\right)_{C} = \frac{0.3560}{2} = 0.17800$$

$$\left(\frac{\Delta T}{W}\right)_{\text{full}} = \frac{0.2245}{3} = 0.07485$$

**against which the two aeroplanes stand at**

$$\frac{0.10286}{0.07485} = 1.374, \qquad \frac{0.17800}{0.07485} = 2.378, \qquad \frac{0.17800}{0.10286} = 1.731$$

An engine-out yaw moment is a thrust asymmetry, so a model with 37 percent more thrust to weight produces a proportionally larger upset than the full-scale aeroplane would at the same flight condition. **Engine-out control was a stated flight-test objective**, tested at low speed, takeoff configuration and minimum operating weight with an outboard engine failed [[Taylor and Vicroy, X-48B flight-test progress overview][research_taylor_x48b_progress]]. **So that particular test was harder than the aeroplane will face, and a pass is conservative.** **The X-48C's engine-out case is harder still, at 2.378 times the full-scale upset**, because losing one engine of two removes half the thrust where losing one of three removes a third, and the C model's thrust to weight is higher as well. That is the pleasant direction for a demonstration to be tilted, and it is the opposite of the direction found in [A332][related_post_a332_lockheed_martin_x35].

## The Two Aircraft

| | X-48B | X-48C |
|---|---|---|
| First flight | 20 July 2007 | 7 August 2012 |
| Last flight | 2010, second phase to 2012 | 9 April 2013 |
| Flights | 92 | 30 |
| Span | 20.4 ft | just over 20 ft |
| Gross weight | 523 to 525 lb | about 500 lb |
| Engines | 3 turbojets, 54 lbf installed each | 2 turbojets, 89 lbf each, planned at 75 |
| Thrust to weight | 0.309 | 0.356 |
| Vertical surfaces | winglets with rudders at the tips | twin tails moved inboard |
| Aft body | as designed | extended about 2 ft |
| Maximum speed | 118 kt | about 140 mph |
| Ceiling | 10,000 ft | 10,000 ft |
| Endurance | 30 to 40 min, 13 gal fuel | comparable |

**The sources disagree about the C model's engines and the disagreement is load-bearing.** NASA's fact sheet gives two engines of 89 pounds thrust, while the programme's own 2010 planning presentation gives two of 75 [[Vicroy, X-48B blended wing body ground to flight correlation update][research_vicroy_correlation]] [[X-48 Hybrid/Blended Wing Body, NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-090][ref_nasa_fs090]]. **The later figure is more likely to describe what was fitted and the earlier to describe what was planned**, and this article uses 89 while reporting both, because the engine-out arithmetic below depends on which is right. **At 75 pounds the thrust to weight is 0.300 rather than 0.356 and the engine-out factor is 2.004 rather than 2.378**, which moves the size of the conclusion and not its direction.

**The C model was a noise aeroplane and its modifications were acoustic in intent.** The winglets were relocated inboard next to the engine exhaust ducts, becoming twin vertical tails, and the aft deck was extended about two feet rearward, both to shield engine noise from the ground [[X-48 Hybrid/Blended Wing Body, NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-090][ref_nasa_fs090]] [[Boeing flies X-48C blended wing body research aircraft][ref_boeing_x48c_release]]. The low-noise configuration descends from NASA's Environmentally Responsible Aviation studies of aircraft two decades ahead [[The Environmentally Responsible Aviation project, a technology development project][research_era_project]].

**Two of those changes work against the axis the programme had already named as weakest.** Moving a vertical surface inboard on a swept planform moves it forward, shortening its moment arm about the centre of gravity, and the aft-deck extension recovers part of that arm rather than adding to it. Separately, losing one engine of two removes half the thrust where losing one of three removes a third. **NASA records that the handling qualities of the C model differed from the B model and that new flight control limiters were written for it**, which is the clearest published statement that the noise modification was not free.

### The X-48C Made the Weak Axis Weaker, and the Arithmetic Says by Roughly How Much

**The programme's own stated hypothesis was that yaw control is poor throughout the flight envelope** [[Taylor and Vicroy, X-48B flight-test progress overview][research_taylor_x48b_progress]]. **The noise modification then acted on that axis twice, in the same direction, and neither action was intended to.**

**The first is the engine count.** The asymmetric thrust fraction computed above rises from 0.10286 to 0.17800, a factor of **1.731** against the B model.

**The second is the moment arm.** Directional authority from a vertical surface scales with the tail volume coefficient,

$$V_v = \frac{S_v \, l_v}{S \, b}$$

in which $l_v$ is the distance from the centre of gravity to the surface's aerodynamic centre. **On a swept planform, moving a surface inboard moves it forward**, because the structure it attaches to sweeps aft with span,

$$\Delta l_v = \Delta y \, \tan \Lambda$$

**The sweep angle of the X-48's outer trailing edge is not published**, so this is evaluated as a sensitivity rather than a result. Taking the winglets from the tip at $y = 10.2$ ft to a station near the exhaust ducts at roughly 2.5 ft, so $\Delta y = 7.7$ ft,

| Assumed sweep | Forward shift | Net after the 2 ft aft-deck extension |
|---|---|---|
| 30 degrees | 4.45 ft | 2.45 ft |
| 35 degrees | 5.39 ft | 3.39 ft |
| 40 degrees | 6.46 ft | 4.46 ft |

**The aft deck was extended about two feet rearward, which acts in the recovering direction**, and that is itself evidence that arm was lost and known to be lost. **Against a tail arm of order ten feet on a twenty-foot aeroplane, a net loss of two to four feet is a reduction in $V_v$ of roughly a quarter to nearly a half**, before any account is taken of the change in surface area or of the interference between a tail and an exhaust plume.

**Both effects push the same way on the axis already named as weakest, and NASA records the consequence.** The project team wrote flight control system modifications for the C model, including limiters to keep it inside a safe envelope, **because its handling qualities differed from the B model's** [[X-48 Hybrid/Blended Wing Body, NASA Dryden Fact Sheet FS-090][ref_nasa_fs090]]. **The arithmetic above is one reading of why.**

## Dependent Systems

### Control Allocation, Which Is How the Aeroplane Is Flown at All

**The X-48B carries twenty individually actuated control surfaces along the trailing edge of the wing and the winglets, and those twenty provide all of its control power** [[Taylor and Vicroy, X-48B flight-test progress overview][research_taylor_x48b_progress]]. There is no horizontal tail and no conventional rudder. Pitch, roll and yaw are produced by blending surfaces that each contribute to more than one axis, and the outboard elevons split into drag rudders for yaw in the manner of the B-2 [[Liebeck, Design of the blended wing body subsonic transport][research_liebeck_bwb]] [[Northrop Grumman B-2 Spirit][ref_b2_wikipedia]].

**An assessment of the dynamic interaction of all twenty surfaces was a stated flight-test objective**, which is an unusual thing to have to schedule and a direct consequence of the configuration.

### The Leading Edge, Flown Both Ways

The design intent required a leading-edge slat on the outboard wing, and the flight programme tested two leading-edge configurations, slats extended and slats retracted, interchangeable between flights. **Bracketing the leading edge is the programme hedging exactly where the scaling is weakest**, whether or not it was framed that way at the time.

### The Ground Station

The aeroplane was flown from a ground station on the north side of Edwards Air Force Base using conventional stick, rudder and throttle, inside an irregular working area whose longest straight dimension is about 5.5 nautical miles. **An aeroplane whose motions run 3.430 times fast, inside 5.5 nautical miles, is a demanding piloting task before any aerodynamics are considered.**

## The Flight Test Record

**The programme flew 122 times, 92 as the X-48B and 30 as the X-48C.** The first two phases, 39 flights from July 2007 to December 2008, are documented in detail and are the basis for what follows [[Taylor and Vicroy, X-48B flight-test progress overview][research_taylor_x48b_progress]].

Testing proceeded in blocks. Envelope expansion came first, then parameter identification, stalls and engine-out work. Three weight configurations were flown, with empty weights of about 395, 405 and 430 pounds, and three centre-of-gravity positions separated by four inches of mean aerodynamic chord. Typical flights lasted 30 to 35 minutes and were limited by a 13-gallon fuel capacity.

**The approach to the limit of controlled flight was made in one-degree increments of angle of attack, descending at idle thrust, which the team judged the lowest-risk condition for probing uncontrollable flight.** At each increment the pilot evaluated controllability in all three axes and performed a pitch-over recovery.

**Phase I did not stop at 39 flights and the fuller picture is better.** The programme ran six blocks to flight 80, alternating slats extended and slats retracted, ending in departure limiter assaults. Its own summary of the phase reports the aeroplane as extremely manoeuvrable in roll, closely matching simulation for up-and-away flight and landing, and the flight control design as very robust [[Vicroy, X-48B blended wing body ground to flight correlation update][research_vicroy_correlation]] [[Taylor, X-48B preliminary flight test results][research_taylor_preliminary]].

**The stall results carry angles, and the difference between the two leading-edge configurations is large.**

$$\alpha_{\text{stall}}^{\text{slats out}} = 24^\circ, \qquad \alpha_{\text{stall}}^{\text{slats in}} = 14^\circ, \qquad \Delta\alpha = 10^\circ$$

**Slats extended, the aeroplane stalled successfully to 24 degrees and remained controllable three degrees beyond the angle of maximum lift.** Slats retracted, it reached 14 degrees. **Ten degrees is not a refinement**, and it is the clearest available measure of how much the leading edge governs this configuration's behaviour, which matters because the leading edge is where the Reynolds sensitivity lives.

**The departure limiter assaults were, in the programme's own words, highly successful.**

**What they found earlier is still the article's most quoted fact.** Just below the predicted stall angle of attack the aeroplane became difficult to hold steady because of a sustained pitch bobble. At a limiting angle of attack the bobble subsided and **the aeroplane departed in uncommanded wing roll-offs**. The limiting angle was reached six times across three flights with three separate pilots in the slats-extended configuration, and twice with slats retracted. **Every pitch-over recovery succeeded.** One pilot described holding the aeroplane near the limit as attempting to balance it on the head of a pin.

**One detail matters more than the rest.** When a pilot attempted to counter the roll-off with lateral stick, the input **slightly delayed the roll-off and then produced a more abrupt wing drop**.

## What the Data Changed

### The Flight Result Contradicts the Design Intent, and the Scaling Says Which to Trust

**Liebeck's published account of the configuration states that separation is initiated in the kink region between the outboard wing and the centrebody, that the outer wing flow remains attached and provides lateral control into the stall regime, and that this is the ideal spanwise location for the stall to begin because the ailerons remain effective and pitch-up is avoided** [[Liebeck, Design of the blended wing body subsonic transport][research_liebeck_bwb]].

**The X-48B found uncommanded wing roll-off, and found that lateral control made it worse.** Those two statements are not compatible. The design intent is that the outboard wing keeps flying and the pilot keeps roll authority. The flight result is that the aeroplane rolls off uncommanded and that using roll authority sharpens the departure.

**The scaling analysis says which of the two the model is entitled to settle, and the answer is neither cleanly.** Separation onset and its spanwise progression are Reynolds-dependent phenomena. At a Reynolds number 1/40.35 of full scale, the model's separation may begin in a different place on the span and at a different angle of attack than the aeroplane's. **The disagreement between design intent and flight observation is therefore exactly the disagreement the scale factor predicts is possible**, and it cannot be resolved by flying the model more.

### NASA Answered the Reynolds Question With a Different Instrument

**The draft of this article argued that the departure boundary is Reynolds-governed and therefore does not transfer from an 8.5 percent model. That is true and it is not the whole story, because the programme never asked the model to carry it alone.**

**The correlation update plots the ground-test campaign on axes of vehicle scale against chord Reynolds number**, and the tests fill the plane [[Vicroy, X-48B blended wing body ground to flight correlation update][research_vicroy_correlation]]. Free-flight, forced-oscillation, rotary, large-angle and free spin and tumble tests sit at small scale and low Reynolds number. Static aerodynamic tests, the Arnold Engineering Development Center 16T tunnel and **the National Transonic Facility sit at Reynolds numbers reaching the full-scale value**. The X-48B flight test is one point on that plane and not the whole of it.

**So the instrument that supplies dynamic fidelity and the instrument that supplies Reynolds number are different instruments, and the programme ran both.** A pressurised cryogenic tunnel buys Reynolds number and cannot fly. A free-flight model flies and cannot buy Reynolds number. **Neither is a substitute for the other and the correlation exercise is what joins them.**

**The programme's own verdict on the free-flight method is favourable.** It records that the free-flight test method provided good correlation with the observed one-g flight test limits, which is the specific claim this article was sceptical of and is evidence against that scepticism.

### The Poor Comparison Was Somewhere Else Entirely

**Asked where the ground-to-flight comparisons were poor, the programme does not name the stall.** It names the pitching moment, and it names a cause that has nothing to do with scaling.

**The magnitude of the support interference effect on pitching moment was much larger than anticipated** [[Vicroy, X-48B blended wing body ground to flight correlation update][research_vicroy_correlation]]. The same configuration measured on a three-inch post with a pitch link and on a 1.2-inch bent sting in the Langley 14 by 22 foot tunnel gave materially different pitching-moment curves. **That is a defect of how the model was held, not of how it was scaled**, and on a tailless aeroplane trimmed by its own trailing edge the pitching moment is the quantity least able to absorb an error.

**A second lesson is administrative and the programme states it plainly.** Ground-to-flight correlation is difficult without a central repository of wind tunnel, flight, computational and simulation data. **That is a data-management finding rather than an aerodynamic one**, and it is the kind of conclusion that only a programme running seven kinds of test on one configuration is in a position to reach.

**The programme also names what it could not compare.** Transonic behaviour, held only in the National Transonic Facility and 16T data, and post-departure modes such as the falling leaf, the spin and the tumble, held only in large-angle, rotary and free spin and tumble data. **Neither has a flight comparison at all**, which is a more precise statement of the article's concern than the article's own was.

### What Transfers and What Does Not

**The division is clean and it follows from which group is matched.**

**Froude-governed and transferable.** The character of the departure as a motion, the number of cycles it takes to develop, whether a pitch-over recovery works, the control law's ability to hold the aeroplane, and the handling qualities of the whole low-speed envelope. **These are dynamics, and dynamics is what the model was built to reproduce.** The programme's claim to have proved low-speed controllability throughout the envelope rests here and is sound.

**Reynolds-governed and not transferable without further argument.** The angle of attack at which the roll-off begins, the spanwise station at which separation starts, the maximum lift coefficient, and whether the slat is required. **These are the properties of a boundary layer** [[Schlichting and Gersten, Boundary layer theory][book_schlichting]], and a model at 1/40.35 of the aeroplane's Reynolds number is not evidence about them. That maximum lift rises with Reynolds number over this range is a standard result [[Hoerner and Borst, Fluid-dynamic lift][book_hoerner_lift]].

**The programme's own objective list asks for both.** It states an objective to determine, via flight manoeuvres and dynamic-scaling relationships, the full-scale low-speed flight characteristics **and departure onset boundaries** [[Taylor and Vicroy, X-48B flight-test progress overview][research_taylor_x48b_progress]]. **The first transfers from the flight vehicle alone and the second does not**, and the difference between them is the whole content of the scale factor.

**What the programme did about that is the part the draft of this article got wrong.** It did not ask the flight vehicle to carry the second. It ran a suite of ground tests spanning three decades of Reynolds number and correlated them, and it reports the free-flight method as agreeing well with the observed flight limits. **The right criticism is not that the programme confused the two, but that the flight vehicle alone is quoted as though it settled both**, which is a fault of how the result is repeated rather than of how it was obtained.

### The Honest Reading of the Programme

**The X-48 validated a control system and a recovery technique for a configuration, on an aeroplane whose departure boundary is its own rather than the full-scale vehicle's.** That is a smaller claim than the flight vehicle is usually credited with and a more defensible one, and **the programme as a whole claims more than the flight vehicle does, correctly**, because it ran the tunnels that the aeroplane could not be.

**The thing that was genuinely unknown in 2000 was whether a control system could keep a large tailless transport inside its envelope and recover it from the edge.** The flight vehicle answered that, and answered it at a scale where the recovery had to work three and a half times faster than it will on the aeroplane. **That is the durable result, and it does not need the departure boundary to be true.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**The reference vehicle's weight is derived and never quoted.** The figure of 854,875 pounds comes from inverting the cube of the scale ratio on the model's own weight. If the model was not weight-scaled with the precision assumed, the number moves and the comparison against Liebeck moves with it.

**The relative density factor is now quantified rather than assumed away, and it moves the answer.** Taking the model's condition at the field elevation of Rogers Dry Lake raises the implied full-scale weight from 854,875 pounds to 914,885, and taking it at the ceiling raises it to 1,157,634. **The record does not state the altitude at which the weight scaling was set**, so 854,875 pounds is reported as a lower bound and every comparison drawn from it inherits that status.

**The BWB-17 does not fit the same arithmetic.** At 6 percent scale and 120 pounds,

$$b_{\text{ref}} = \frac{17}{0.06} = 283\ \text{ft}, \qquad W_{\text{full}} = \frac{120}{0.06^{3}} = 555{,}556\ \text{lb}$$

**That does not match Liebeck's 823,000 pounds**, so either the BWB-17 answered to an earlier and lighter reference design or it was not weight-scaled to the vehicle described in the same paper. **The record does not say which**, and this article does not guess.

**The wing area is not stated by any primary source consulted, and one section now depends on it.** The figure of 100.5 square feet comes from a secondary compilation. It enters only through the reference chord $c = S/b$ used to put the Reynolds numbers on an absolute footing, and **the ratio of 40.35 does not depend on it at all**, because the chord cancels between model and full scale. **A reader who distrusts the area should discard the two absolute Reynolds figures and keep everything else**, which is why the ratio and not the absolute value carries the argument.

**The X-48C's moment-arm loss is a sensitivity and not a measurement.** No source consulted publishes the sweep of the outer trailing edge, the spanwise station of the C model's twin tails, or the vertical surface areas of either aeroplane. **The inboard station of 2.5 feet and the tail arm of order ten feet are assumptions**, chosen to be plausible rather than derived, and the tabulated shifts move with them. **What does not move is the sign**, since the geometry admits no reading in which moving a surface inboard on an aft-swept planform lengthens its arm. **The engine-count half of the same argument is exact**, resting only on published thrusts and weights.

**The claim that departure onset does not transfer from the flight vehicle is an argument from the scaling relations and not a measurement.** No source consulted states a full-scale departure angle of attack, so there is nothing to compare the model's limiting angle against. **A quantified Reynolds correction is not attempted**, because it depends on the configuration's separation behaviour, which is the unknown in question.

**The draft of this article stated that claim more strongly than the record supports, and the primary pass corrected it.** The programme ran high-Reynolds tunnel tests precisely to cover the gap, and reports its free-flight method as correlating well with observed flight limits. **The article no longer says the departure boundary was left to the model**, because it was not.

**The correlation update is a conference presentation rather than a technical report**, so its findings arrive as summary lines without the data behind them. **The stall angles of 24 and 14 degrees, the phrase about departure limiter assaults and the pitching-moment finding are quoted from slides**, and a reader wanting the supporting curves will not find them there.

**The X-48C's engine thrust is stated differently by two sources**, 89 pounds in the fact sheet and 75 in the 2010 presentation. **Every engine-out figure for the C model moves with that choice**, from 2.378 down to 2.004 against the full-scale trijet. **The direction of the conclusion does not move** and the size of it does.

**The full-scale thrust comparison uses Liebeck's second-generation design and not the reference vehicle.** The 0.2245 thrust-to-weight figure belongs to an 823,000-pound, 800-passenger commercial design. **If the military reference vehicle is thrustier, the model's 1.374 excess shrinks**, and the engine-out conservatism shrinks with it.

### Other aeronautical and scaling literature

**The residual, reported and not hidden.** On-subject aeronautical work belonging to no cluster above, including flight control hardware, icing, air data, agility metrics and a long tail of single-topic papers. **A residual near a quarter is a property of a subject that spans aerodynamics, flight dynamics, scaling and acoustics at once**, and shrinking it by inventing headings would describe the filing rather than the field.

### Aerodynamics of the configuration

**The flow the vehicle lives in.** Lift, drag, vortex behaviour, boundary layers, computation and wind tunnel technique. **The X-48's aerodynamic question is a low-speed one**, which is unusual in this series, because the cruise case was never in doubt and the approach and the stall were.

**The configuration itself, and the largest cluster after the residual.** Planform definition, centrebody structure, the non-circular pressure vessel, spanload and the trade against the tube and wing. **This cluster grew by a third when the gate stopped letting a hyphen defeat it**, because the literature writes blended-wing-body hyphenated far more often than not.

### Stall, departure and the uncommanded roll-off

**The subject of the article's central finding.** Maximum lift, separation onset, wing drop, departure boundaries and recovery. **This is the cluster the scaling argument bears on**, since separation onset is the phenomenon a Froude-scaled model reproduces least faithfully and the one this aeroplane was built to find.

### Tailless stability and control, and directional authority

**What a configuration without a tail gives up.** Directional stability, vertical surface sizing, yaw authority and the Dutch roll. **The programme's own hypothesis was that yaw control is poor throughout the envelope**, and the X-48C then moved the vertical surfaces inboard.

**How the aeroplane was actually flown.** Ground stations, displays, link behaviour and the pilot who is not aboard. **This matters more here than in most of the series**, because Froude scaling compresses the aeroplane's time while leaving the pilot's reaction time exactly where it was.

### Control allocation and redundant control effectors

**Twenty surfaces and one pilot.** Allocation, blending, daisy chaining and the overactuated problem. **The X-48B carries twenty individually actuated trailing-edge surfaces**, so allocation is not a refinement here but the means by which the aeroplane is controlled at all.

## The Source Base

**The survey rests on 7,416 research records assembled from Crossref, the NASA Technical Reports Server and the Defense Technical Information Center**, of which 1,311 are report primaries, being 17.7 percent. **Thirteen further primaries are cited by identifier rather than left to the sweep to find**, and the primary pass added nine of those thirteen.

### The Definition of Primary Was Wrong and It Was Wrong in a Measurable Way

**Primacy was being inherited from whichever sweep returned the record, and it is a property of the document.** A Defense Technical Information Center report carries a Crossref-registered digital object identifier under the 10.21236 prefix, so the same report is returned by the DTIC sweep and by the Crossref sweep, under two different labels.

**101 urls in the pool were held twice under two labels, and deduplication kept the Crossref label for 95 of them.** Each of those is a report primary that was counted as secondary. **A further 38 arrived only through Crossref and so never carried the primary label at all**, giving 133 in total.

**Primacy is now derived from the identifier**, being an NTRS url or the DTIC prefix, which is the corpus rule about recomputing rather than inheriting applied to provenance instead of to arithmetic.

### The Equation Pass Promoted Five Subjects and the Pool Held Three of Them

**The four-pass rhythm has no step that re-asks whether an absent subject has become load-bearing**, and the audit at the head of this pass is the only thing that can. A344 recorded an atmosphere cluster of two as correct and its equation pass then made the atmosphere necessary. **A345's equation pass did the same thing five times.**

| Subject the equation pass made load-bearing | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| the standard atmosphere itself | 60 | 83 |
| viscosity and its variation with temperature | 0 | **0** |
| the relative density factor and model mass scaling | 1 | 21 |
| vertical tail sizing and the volume coefficient | 106 | 145 |
| engine-out and asymmetric thrust | 4 | 21 |
| Reynolds effect on maximum lift specifically | 529 | 603 |
| dynamic scaling as a method | 120 | 145 |

**Each thin subject was broadened before being called thin**, moving viscosity from 0 to 2, the relative density factor from 1 to 7 and engine-out from 4 to 8, which establishes that these were pool gaps rather than pattern defects. **That is the discipline A343's publication review failed in the opposite direction**, by assuming two real gaps were artefacts.

### Viscosity Stayed at Zero and That Is the Fourth Kind of Thin

**Six targeted queries across three sources returned 421 records mentioning viscosity or transport properties, and the aeronautical gate admitted 14.** The remainder are lubricating oils, canola oil, molten metals, protein solutions, supercooled sucrose and ASTM Saybolt conversion tables.

**The gate is refusing them correctly and no loosening of it would help.** The viscosity of air as a function of temperature is not an under-served subject. **It was settled by Sutherland in 1893 and has lived in tables ever since** [[Sutherland, The viscosity of gases and molecular force][research_sutherland_viscosity]] [[U.S. Standard Atmosphere, 1976][research_us_standard_atmosphere]] [[The NBS-NACA tables of thermal properties of gases][research_nbs_naca_tables]].

**This is the fourth kind of thin, which is a subject whose vocabulary does not discriminate**, compounded by the third, which is a subject so settled it stopped generating papers. **A bibliographic sweep is the wrong instrument for a tabulated physical constant**, and the remedy is to know the document exists and fetch it by identifier.

### The Harvest Never Asked for the Aeroplane by Name

**The first harvest asked for the subject matter and never named the X-48.** That is why the four documents the whole argument rests on had to be cited by identifier, and it looked like foresight when it was covering for a gap.

**A supplementary harvest naming the aeroplane returned eight further programme documents**, including the two that changed this article. **One is the ground-to-flight correlation update, which answers the article's keystone question directly** and which the draft argued without [[Vicroy, X-48B blended wing body ground to flight correlation update][research_vicroy_correlation]]. **The other reports the phase-one flight results with the stall angles attached** [[Taylor, X-48B preliminary flight test results][research_taylor_preliminary]] [[Goldthorpe, Rossitto and Hyde, X-48B blended wing body flight test performance of maximum sideslip and high to post stall angle-of-attack command tracking][research_goldthorpe_poststall]].

**A near-miss is worth recording because it is this article's own subject.** A first measurement reported zero records naming the X-48 in a pool of six thousand, and that was going to be stated as a fact about indexing. **The pattern was `\bX-?48\b`, and a word boundary after `48` cannot match `X-48B`, because the next character is a letter.** The records had been there all along. **An article about a hyphen defeating a gate nearly shipped a claim produced by a word boundary defeating a probe.**

### Three Gate Passes and Then a Merge, Because a Correction Changes the Instrument

| Stage | Pool | Report primaries | Fraction |
|---|---|---|---|
| draft, separator defect present | 6,395 | | |
| draft, separator flattening in the gate | 6,456 | | |
| draft, weak anchor narrowed | 6,428 | 796 | 13.0 percent |
| primary pass, duplicates collapsed and merged | 7,693 | 1,311 | 17.7 percent |

**The primary pass added 1,366 records and removed 101 duplicate urls**, and the arithmetic is printed by the merge rather than asserted.

**The definition of primary still excludes the AIAA conference papers that are among the most important sources here.** Three of the article's central documents are AIAA papers written by the people who flew the aeroplane, and no metric keyed on publisher will call them primary. **17.7 percent is a lower bound on how much of this survey is first-hand**, and the thirteen identifier-cited primaries are the ones that actually carry the argument.

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

The dates, the flight counts, the two configurations, the builder, the engine fits, the modification list for the X-48C and the block structure of the flight test programme are taken from NASA and Boeing publications and from the two AIAA papers. The uncommanded wing roll-off, the behaviour of lateral stick during it, the six and two occurrences in the two slat configurations and the successful pitch-over recoveries are reported in the flight-test progress paper. The stall angles of 24 and 14 degrees, the controllability three degrees beyond maximum lift, the six-block structure of phase one to flight 80, the description of the departure limiter assaults as highly successful, the plot of ground tests on axes of vehicle scale against chord Reynolds number, the finding that support interference on pitching moment was much larger than anticipated, the statement that the free-flight method correlated well with observed flight limits, and the list of comparisons never made are reported in the ground-to-flight correlation update and the preliminary results presentation.

### Verified by Independent Derivation

The scale factor of 0.085000 from the published span and reference span. The Froude ratio table. The time compression of 3.430 and the Reynolds penalty of 40.35. The comparison against the X-36 at 1.815 and 5.979. The ladder of three candidate vehicles and the factor of 2.247 in Reynolds number attributable to the X-48A cancellation. The implied full-scale weight of 854,875 pounds and its ratio of 1.160 against Liebeck's design scaled to the same span. The thrust-to-weight figures of 0.3086 and 0.2245 and their ratio of 1.374. The asymmetric thrust fractions of 0.10286, 0.17800 and 0.07485 and the ratios of 1.374, 2.378 and 1.731 that follow. The absolute Reynolds numbers of $6.24 \times 10^6$ and $2.52 \times 10^8$ at the stated reference chord. The kinematic viscosity ratio of 1.281 between 10,000 feet and sea level on the standard atmosphere, and the effective penalty of 51.7 that follows. The implied full-scale weights of 914,885 and 1,157,634 pounds at the two non-unity readings of the relative density factor. The full-scale equivalent speed of 404.7 knots. The BWB-17's implied reference span of 283 feet and weight of 555,556 pounds.

### Analysis

The division of the flight results into Froude-governed conclusions that transfer and Reynolds-governed conclusions that do not. The identification of the disagreement between Liebeck's stated stall progression and the observed roll-off as the disagreement the scale factor predicts. The reading of the engine-out test as conservative because the model is over-thrusted. The geometric argument that moving a vertical surface inboard on a swept planform shortens its moment arm, and the tabulated sensitivity of that shift to an assumed sweep angle. The reading of the X-48C as doubly penalised on its weakest axis, by engine count exactly and by moment arm approximately.

### Inference

That the reference vehicle is a military freighter rather than a commercial airliner, inferred from the implied weight being 1.160 times a passenger design of the same span and corroborated by the Air Force's stated interest. That bracketing the leading edge with two slat configurations hedges the Reynolds uncertainty, which is a reading of the test matrix and not a stated rationale.

### Corrected During This Article's Own Passes

The draft argued that the departure boundary was left to the flight vehicle alone. **It was not**, and the primary pass found the document that says so. The programme ran a suite of ground tests spanning three decades of Reynolds number, including the National Transonic Facility, and reports its free-flight method as correlating well with the observed flight limits. The article's criticism now falls on how the flight result is repeated rather than on how it was obtained.

### What the Record Does Not Settle

The reference vehicle's actual weight, span aside. The wing area from a primary source. The positions of the vertical surfaces on either aeroplane. The full-scale departure angle of attack. Whether the BWB-17's weight answers to the design published alongside it. Whether the X-48C's noise objective was met, which is an acoustic result this article does not have.

## Out of Scope

The acoustic measurements and the shielding result of the X-48C, which need a noise dataset this article does not have. The structural design of the non-circular pressure vessel, which is the configuration's hardest problem and is not a flight-dynamics subject. The economics of the blended wing body against the tube and wing. The later Boeing and NASA transonic truss-braced and blended configurations that followed the X-48. The military airlift requirement that motivated Air Force interest.

## Conclusion

**The X-48 is the aeroplane in this series whose most interesting property is its size.** It flew 122 times, it was controllable throughout the low-speed envelope, it departed in uncommanded wing roll-offs at a limiting angle of attack, and it recovered every time. **All four of those statements are true of a 20.4-foot aeroplane, and only three of them are evidence about a 240-foot one.**

**The one that does not carry is the departure boundary, and it is the one a reader most wants.** A free-flight model buys dynamic fidelity by surrendering Reynolds number, and at 8.5 percent the surrender is a factor of 40.35. Separation onset is precisely what that factor governs, and the flight programme's most quoted single result is a separation phenomenon.

**The programme was not naive about this and its own record is the proof.** It flew both leading-edge configurations, which bracket the behaviour the scale factor makes least certain, and it plotted its ground tests on axes of scale against Reynolds number and filled the plane, up to and including the National Transonic Facility. **The instrument that flies and the instrument that reaches Reynolds number are different instruments, and the programme ran both.**

**The disagreement this article began with survives that.** The design paper says the outer wing keeps flying into the stall and the ailerons stay effective. The flight report says the aeroplane rolls off uncommanded and that roll input makes it worse. **No amount of flying the model resolves that**, and the programme's own list of what it could not compare puts post-departure behaviour first.

**What the X-48 proved is that a control system can hold a large tailless transport at low speed and recover it from its own edge, three and a half times faster than the aeroplane will have to.** In 2000 that was the open question and it is no longer.

**The most useful thing in the record is not a result but a lesson about instruments.** Asked where its ground-to-flight comparisons were poor, the programme does not name the stall or the scale factor. It names the support that held the model in the tunnel. **A campaign that spent six years and 122 flights worrying about Reynolds number was caught out by a three-inch post**, and that is worth more to the next programme than any number in this article.
